why:
An AI engineer’s most important work often depends on people they cannot instruct. You build an evaluation suite that would catch regressions before release, but each product team decides whether to run it. You find that the research team’s benchmark does not reflect real traffic, but they own their release criteria. You believe the company should stop sending customer data to a third-party model, but that decision belongs to product, legal and security. You know a junior colleague is stuck, but you are not their manager. In each case, being right is not enough. Something only changes if you can get other people to act.

This is what interviewers mean by leadership when they ask individual contributors about it, and it is why the theme comes up in almost every loop, not only for managers. Google’s guide to structured interviewing lists leadership as one of the attributes it assesses and describes the individual-contributor version as “emergent leadership”: taking initiative, working collaboratively across teams and driving your own development. Its candidate tips ask applicants to think about how they have used communication and decision-making skills to mobilise others, “by helping a team succeed even when you weren’t officially the leader”. Amazon’s list of example behavioural questions includes “Share an example of when you took the lead on a project” and “What did you do to motivate a group or encourage collaboration on a team project?”.

Candidates find these questions hard for two opposite reasons. Some have never had a leadership title and conclude they have no leadership stories, when in fact they have led projects, set standards and helped colleagues. Others tell leadership stories that are really stories about being right and pushing until others gave in, which interviewers score as stubbornness rather than influence.

This lesson explains what influence without authority actually consists of: mapping the people involved and their incentives, building a case in their terms, lowering the cost of saying yes, and earning the credibility that makes people listen. It covers leading a project when you are not anyone’s manager, mentoring stories, the specific influence problems AI engineers face between research, product and engineering, and how scope changes with level. The worked example answers “Tell me about a time you got another team to adopt something you built”, weakly and strongly, sentence by sentence.
primer:
A good model is the maintainer of an open-source library. A maintainer cannot order anyone to use their library, contribute to it or follow its conventions. Yet good maintainers shape what thousands of people do. They do it by solving a real problem people have, making adoption easy (clear documentation, sensible defaults, migration guides), being reliable (releases that do not break things, responses to issues), listening to users and changing the library when users are right, and giving visible credit to contributors. Influence without authority inside a company works the same way. You are the maintainer of an idea, a tool or a standard, and the other teams are your users.

The analogy breaks in one place: inside a company, there usually is someone with authority over the decision, even if it is not you. A product manager decides priorities, a research lead decides release criteria, a director can settle a disagreement between teams. So influence at work has an extra lever the open-source maintainer lacks: making sure the right decision-maker sees a fair, clear case at the right time.

Seen this way, influence is less a personality trait than a set of habits anyone can practise.

The levers of influence, roughly in the order you build them, are shown below.

The order matters. Credibility is built before you need it, through delivering reliably and being straight with people. Understanding the other team’s incentives comes before you design your proposal, because a proposal that ignores what they are measured on will be politely ignored. Evidence persuades when it speaks to their concerns, not yours. A written case lets people consider it on their own time and forward it to whoever decides. Lowering the cost of saying yes (doing the hard first part yourself, offering a small pilot) turns “maybe later” into “sure, let’s try”. And allies and shared credit let the change spread beyond the people you personally persuade.

It is worth noticing what this model leaves out. It has no place for seniority, volume or persistence. Seniority helps, because it brings credibility, but people with titles fail to influence all the time when they ignore the other levers. Volume and persistence (repeating your case louder and more often) mostly produce resistance: the other side starts defending their position rather than considering yours. Persistence has a role only in the gentler sense of patience: keeping a good idea alive until the evidence or the timing makes it easy to accept. Candidates whose stories rely on persistence alone often describe themselves, without meaning to, as someone colleagues learned to avoid.

Interviewers listen for these moves. A story in which you understood the other team’s concerns, offered a pilot, did the integration work yourself and credited their champion is unmistakably a leadership story, whatever your title was.
body:
1. The questions and what they test

Leadership questions take several forms, and it helps to recognise them:

Question formWhat it tests
Tell me about a time you led a project.Organising work and people: goals, roles, decisions, communication, unblocking.
Tell me about influencing someone without authority.Persuasion through evidence, incentives and trust, across teams.
Tell me about getting a team to adopt something.Driving change: lowering adoption cost, pilots, champions.
Tell me about a time you motivated a group.Creating shared purpose and momentum, especially in difficult periods.
Tell me about mentoring someone.Developing others: coaching, feedback, giving stretch opportunities.
Tell me about setting technical direction.Senior-level leadership: choosing what the team should build and why.

The behaviours interviewers score are fairly consistent across them: initiative (you started something), clarity (people knew what to do), respect for others’ expertise and decisions, effective persuasion, enabling others rather than doing everything yourself, resilience when people resisted, and a result that came about through other people’s actions. Google’s manager research, Project Oxygen, is a useful reference even for individual contributors: among the ten behaviours it found in effective managers are being a good coach, empowering the team without micromanaging, communicating effectively, having a clear vision and strategy, and collaborating across the company. Most of these are things an individual contributor can show too.

2. Map the people before you make the case

Influence starts with understanding who is involved. For any change you want, there are typically four kinds of people: those who decide (the product manager who owns the roadmap, the research lead who owns release criteria), those who are affected (the teams who would have to change their workflow), those who can block (security, legal, a platform team whose approval is needed), and potential allies (people who already feel the problem). A simple stakeholder map places each person by how much they can influence the outcome and how much it affects them.

For the people who matter most, find out what they are measured on and worried about. A research lead may be measured on model quality metrics and publication; a PM on launches and user metrics; a platform team on reliability and cost. Your proposal will land much better if it helps their measures, or at least does not hurt them. “This evaluation gate will slow your releases” is a threat to a research team’s incentives; “this evaluation gate catches the regressions that caused the last two rollbacks, which cost your team three weeks” is help.

3. Build the case in their terms, and write it down

A persuasive case usually has the same parts: the problem, with evidence in the other side’s terms; the proposal; the alternatives you considered and why you prefer this one; the costs and risks, stated honestly; and a specific, small ask. Writing it down, as a short design document or one-page proposal, has big advantages over arguing in meetings. People can read it when they have time, think rather than react, forward it to the person who decides, and respond to specifics. It also forces you to state the case precisely, which often improves it.

Evidence persuades best when it is concrete and close to the reader’s experience. For an AI team, that might be: five real cases where the current evaluation passed a model that then failed in production, each with what it cost; a chart of rollback frequency; a quote from a support lead about a bad week. Abstract arguments (“best practice says we should evaluate on production data”) persuade far less than “here are the three regressions in the last quarter that this would have caught”.

Address objections before they are raised. If you know the research team worries about release delays, state the expected added time and how you will keep it small. Showing you have understood the other side’s concerns is itself persuasive; it tells them you are proposing something workable, not something that serves only you.

4. Lower the cost of saying yes

Many good proposals fail not because people disagree but because saying yes would cost them time they do not have. The most effective influence move is often to absorb that cost yourself:

  • Do the hard first part: build the integration, write the migration, set up the first evaluation run for them.
  • Offer a pilot: one team, one model, one month, with a clear way out. A pilot turns a big decision into a small, reversible one (a two-way door, in beh6’s terms).
  • Start with the willing: find the team that already feels the problem most, make them successful, and let their success persuade the next team. Peers persuade peers better than you can.
  • Make the default easy: a template, a one-line configuration, a shared library, so that doing the right thing is the path of least resistance.

In interview stories these moves are very recognisable, and they distinguish influence from persuasion. “I convinced them” tells the interviewer little. “I wrote the integration for their pipeline myself so that adopting it was a one-line change, and offered to run it in shadow mode for two weeks before they relied on it” tells them you know how change actually happens.

5. Credibility: built before you need it

People listen to those they trust, and trust at work comes from a few sources: expertise (you clearly know the subject), a record of delivering (you have done what you said before), dependability (you do what you say, on time), straightness (you say what you know and what you do not, and you report problems early), and generosity (you help others and give credit). Google’s Project Aristotle found dependability to be one of the five dynamics of effective teams, alongside psychological safety, structure and clarity, meaning and impact.

The key point for stories is that credibility is usually built before the influence moment. A strong influence story often contains a sentence about it: “I’d spent my first two months fixing the flaky parts of their data pipeline, so when I proposed the new evaluation gate they already trusted that I wasn’t going to slow them down.” That sentence shows the interviewer you understand influence as a long game.

6. Leading a project without being a manager

Many engineers lead projects as a tech lead or project owner without managing anyone. Leading in that role is mostly about making four things clear and keeping them clear:

  • Goals: what the project is for and how success will be measured (beh6’s problem statement).
  • Roles: who owns which part, and who decides what.
  • Decisions: making sure decisions are made by the right people at the right time, and recorded, often in a simple decision log, so settled questions stay settled.
  • Progress and risk: a regular, honest view of where things stand, with problems raised early.

Then the lead’s main job is to unblock: chasing dependencies, resolving disagreements (beh4), getting decisions from people outside the team, and protecting the team from distractions. A common weak project-leadership story shows the lead doing most of the technical work personally. A strong one shows the lead making it possible for everyone else to do their best work, and still contributing technically where it mattered most.

7. Developing others

Mentoring and developing colleagues is leadership, and for senior individual contributors it is usually an explicit expectation. Being a good coach is the first of Project Oxygen’s ten manager behaviours, and Amazon’s Hire and Develop the Best principle says “Leaders develop leaders and take seriously their role in coaching others.”

A strong mentoring story is specific about three things. The starting point: what the person struggled with, described respectfully (“she was strong technically but tended to take on vague tasks without clarifying them, and lost days as a result”). The actions: what you did, ideally things that built their judgement rather than solving problems for them, such as asking questions instead of giving answers, giving a stretch assignment with support, specific feedback after each attempt, and stepping back as they improved. And the change: something visible in their work, such as leading a project on their own, a promotion, or a manager’s comment. Avoid mentoring stories that make the other person sound incompetent or that centre on how much you knew.

8. Influence in AI work: research, product and engineering

AI engineers often sit between groups with different cultures and incentives, which makes influence both harder and more valuable. Researchers tend to value novelty and benchmark results; product teams value user outcomes and launch dates; platform and infrastructure teams value reliability and cost; security, privacy and legal teams value risk reduction. Common influence situations include persuading researchers to evaluate on production-like data, persuading product to invest in evaluation and monitoring rather than features, persuading platform teams to support a new serving pattern, and persuading leadership to accept a slower but safer launch.

The same levers apply in each case, but translation is the special skill: expressing an engineering concern in the other group’s currency. To a researcher, a production regression is a threat to the credibility of their result. To a product manager, missing evaluation is a risk to the launch date and to user trust. To leadership, a safety gap is a reputational and legal risk with a probability and a cost. Candidates who show they can translate like this demonstrate exactly the cross-functional leadership AI teams struggle to find.

9. Motivating a group

Amazon’s example question “What did you do to motivate a group or encourage collaboration on a team project?” asks about a different kind of leadership: not changing a decision, but changing energy and focus. Typical situations are a team demoralised after a failed launch, a long project in its tedious middle, a group from several teams that does not yet feel like a team, or a crunch before a deadline.

The behaviours that work in such stories are concrete, not inspirational speeches. Connecting the work to its purpose: showing the team real user conversations the assistant had improved, or the support lead’s message about time saved. Meaning and impact are two of the five team dynamics in Google’s Project Aristotle, and engineers often never see the effect of their work. Making progress visible: a weekly evaluation chart that shows the error rate falling, so a long slog has visible milestones. Clearing friction: removing the flaky test, the slow review cycle or the unclear ownership that is quietly draining the team. Recognising contributions specifically: naming what someone did and why it mattered, in front of people whose opinion they value. Protecting the team: pushing back on a new request so the team can finish what matters.

A strong motivation story names the starting state with evidence (“two people had asked to move teams; velocity had halved”), describes two or three of these specific actions, and gives a change you could observe: delivery recovered, people stayed, the team asked to keep a practice you introduced. Avoid stories that amount to “I stayed positive”; positivity is not an action anyone can score.

10. Leading in an incident

Incidents create some of the clearest leadership moments, because roles are unclear, pressure is high and someone has to organise people quickly. In many engineering organisations an incident has a designated coordinator, sometimes called the incident commander, whose job is not to fix the problem personally but to make sure it gets fixed: assigning who investigates what, keeping a running record, deciding when to roll back, and communicating with stakeholders. Google’s SRE book describes this kind of role-based incident management in its chapter on managing incidents.

An AI engineer might lead in an incident such as a model producing harmful or wrong outputs at scale, a provider outage, or a cost spike. A strong story shows the candidate creating order: separating investigation from communication, making a fast reversible decision (roll back first, investigate second), keeping stakeholders informed at regular intervals, and running the follow-up postmortem (beh5). It is a leadership story precisely because the candidate’s main contribution was coordination, which interviewers recognise as a skill many strong individual engineers lack.

11. Worked example: getting another team to adopt something

The question, from an interviewer assessing influence and leadership: “Tell me about a time you got another team to adopt something you built.” Both answers are illustrative examples written for this lesson; the people, company and numbers are invented.

Weak answer (about 2 minutes):

What the candidate saysWhat the interviewer writesSignal or noise
“I built an evaluation framework for LLM features that was much better than what other teams were using.”“Built eval framework; claims ‘much better’.”Weak signal: a claim about quality.
“I presented it at the engineering all-hands and explained why everyone should use it.”“Presented at all-hands.”Weak signal: broadcast, not influence.
“Some teams were resistant, they said they didn’t have time, which was frustrating because it would obviously save them time.”“Resistance: no time. Candidate dismissive.”Negative signal: did not engage with the reason.
“So I kept bringing it up in meetings and eventually got my director to mandate it.”“Persisted; director mandated.”Weak to negative: authority substituted for influence.
“Now all the teams use it.”“All teams use (mandated).”Weak: adoption by mandate, no measure of value.

The story shows building and broadcasting, then using a director’s authority when persuasion failed. There is no understanding of the other teams, no lowering of their cost, no evidence and no credit. Likely score: borderline at best for influence.

Strong answer (about 2 minutes 40 seconds):

What the candidate saysWhat the interviewer writesSignal or noise
(S, 15 s) “I’d built an evaluation harness for our team’s LLM features that ran every prompt or model change against a set sampled from production. Two other product teams shipped LLM features with only manual spot checks.”“Own eval harness; 2 other teams on manual checks.”Signal: context and the gap.
(T, 10 s) “I didn’t own their processes, but their regressions were landing in a shared support queue, so I wanted them to adopt it.”“No authority; shared outcome motivates.”Signal: influence without authority, with a reason.
(A, 25 s) “I started by asking each team’s tech lead what stopped them. Both said the same: setting up evaluation sets took weeks they didn’t have, and they worried it would slow releases.”“Asked first; learned blockers = setup cost + release speed.”Strong signal: understanding incentives before proposing.
(A, 30 s) “So I offered to build the first evaluation set for one team myself, from 300 of their real conversations, and made the harness run in under ten minutes so it wouldn’t slow their releases.”“Absorbed setup cost; addressed speed concern (<10 min).”Strong signal: lowering the cost of yes.
(A, 25 s) “We ran it in shadow mode for three weeks, not blocking anything. It flagged two regressions their spot checks had missed, one of which would have broken their citations for every answer.”“Pilot, shadow mode; caught 2 missed regressions.”Strong signal: reversible pilot producing evidence.
(A, 20 s) “Their tech lead presented those results at our cross-team review rather than me, and the second team asked to join the next week.”“Let champion present; peer-driven spread.”Strong signal: credit and coalition.
(R, 20 s) “Within two months all three teams gated releases on it, and regressions reaching the support queue fell from about six a month to one.”“3 teams gated; regressions ~6 → 1/month.”Strong signal: measured outcome of adoption.
(L, 10 s) “What I learned: ask what’s stopping people before you pitch, and do the expensive first step for them.”“Specific lesson.”Signal: reflection.

Likely follow-ups: “What would you have done if the pilot had found nothing?” (kept it running a little longer, then accepted that their spot checks might be enough for their risk level), “Why let their tech lead present?” (peers persuade peers, and it made the result theirs), and “Did anyone still resist?” (an honest answer either way is fine).
deep:
What Project Oxygen implies for individual contributors

Google’s Project Oxygen analysed more than 10,000 data points from performance reviews, feedback surveys and interviews, and found that teams with highly effective managers were more likely to achieve better results, be happier and have lower turnover. Its ten behaviours are written for managers, but several are the core of individual-contributor leadership too: being a good coach, empowering others without micromanaging, communicating effectively, having a clear vision and strategy, having key technical skills, collaborating across the company and making strong decisions. When you prepare leadership stories, it is worth checking which of these each story shows. A senior engineer whose stories show coaching, a clear technical vision and cross-company collaboration is showing the same behaviours Google found in its best managers, which is exactly the signal a senior or staff interviewer wants.

Influence versus manipulation

Interviewers occasionally probe the ethics of influence, and it is worth having a clear view. Legitimate influence changes someone’s decision by improving their information, aligning the proposal with their real interests, and making action easier, all openly; if they later learned exactly how you persuaded them, they would not feel tricked. Manipulation works through hidden information, misrepresented evidence, manufactured urgency or exploiting someone’s position. Besides being wrong, manipulation is ineffective over time, because influence depends on credibility and manipulation spends it. A useful test when telling a story: would the person you influenced be comfortable hearing your account of it? If yes, it was influence.

When influence fails

Not every attempt succeeds, and stories of failed influence can be strong evidence if told well. Influence fails for recognisable reasons: the proposal did not serve the other side’s goals; the evidence was in your terms, not theirs; the ask was too big; the timing was wrong (they were mid-crisis); you went to the decision-maker too late, or too early, before the affected team was on board; or the other side was simply right. A mature failed-influence story identifies which reason applied, shows that you accepted the decision and committed (beh4), and names what you do differently now. Sometimes the best ending is that you were persuaded instead, which shows the openness that makes people willing to listen to you next time.

Writing scales influence

Spoken persuasion reaches the people in the room; writing reaches everyone the document is forwarded to, including the people who decide. Several large companies formalise this. Amazon’s candidate guidance explains that it uses narrative memos instead of slide decks, read silently at the start of meetings, and that these are “a big part of how we share ideas and make decisions”. Engineering organisations widely use design documents for the same purpose. For senior and staff candidates especially, a story that includes a well-received written proposal shows a scalable form of influence. It also gives you concrete detail for follow-ups: what the document argued, who reviewed it, what changed after review.

Influencing upward

Influencing your own manager or leadership is a special case. You have a relationship and regular access, but they hold authority over you, and disagreeing with them carries more perceived risk. The same levers work, with two adjustments. First, framing in their terms means framing in terms of what they are accountable for: their team’s goals, their commitments to their own manager, the risks they will be asked about. Second, timing and channel matter more: raise ideas in a one-to-one before a group setting, bring a written proposal they can forward, and give them options rather than a single demand, so the decision remains theirs. A story about successfully changing a manager’s plan, told with respect for their position and with the outcome, is strong evidence for senior roles, because it shows you will improve decisions above you rather than just execute them.

Leading through others’ credit

One of the clearest markers of senior leadership is comfort with other people getting the visible credit. In the worked example, the candidate let the other team’s tech lead present the pilot results. That choice made the change more likely to succeed (peers trust peers), made the other lead an owner rather than a recipient, and built a relationship for future work. Interviewers notice this, but only if you tell them, which creates a small paradox: you need to describe, briefly and factually, how you deliberately shared credit, without making the story about your generosity. “Their lead presented the results, which helped it spread” does it in a sentence.

Staff-level leadership: choosing the problem

At staff level and above, the hardest leadership work is choosing what an organisation should work on, not executing a chosen project. Stories at this level show a candidate noticing a pattern across teams (every team building its own evaluation tooling, inconsistent safety reviews, duplicated retrieval infrastructure), making the case for a shared direction, aligning several leaders with different incentives, and then letting others lead the pieces. The evidence is about reach and durability: how many teams changed course, and whether the direction outlived the candidate’s direct involvement. If you are interviewing at this level, make sure at least two of your stories show this shape, and make the scope explicit.
prod:
How leadership answers go wrong

Leadership as title. “I haven’t been a manager, so I don’t have a leadership story.” Fix: look for times you led a project, set a standard others adopted, unblocked a cross-team problem or helped a colleague grow.

“I told them.” Influence described as instruction or broadcasting: presentations, emails, insisting. Fix: describe how you understood their needs, built evidence in their terms and lowered their cost.

Authority as a substitute. The story resolves when a manager mandates the change. That may be appropriate, but it is not influence. Fix: if escalation was needed, show what you did before and after it, and why it was the right call (beh4).

The solo hero. A project-leadership story where the lead did all the work. Fix: show how you organised others, and what they achieved.

No resistance. Everyone agreed immediately. Fix: choose a story with real resistance, or describe the indifference you had to overcome.

Credit hoarding. “I drove adoption across the organisation” with no mention of anyone else. Fix: name the roles of the people who helped, and the champion in each team.

Finding leadership stories you already have

Many engineers have more leadership stories than they think. Look for: a time you noticed a problem across teams and organised a fix; a design document you wrote that changed a plan; a standard, template or tool others adopted; an onboarding guide or training you created; a new team member you helped get productive; a project where you coordinated people from several teams; an incident you coordinated; a time you convinced someone senior to change course. Each can be a leadership story if you tell your part in it: the initiative, the organising, the persuasion and the result through others.

Calibrating scope to level

Interviewers read level from the reach of your leadership. For mid-level roles, leading a project within your team or mentoring a new hire is solid evidence. For senior roles, they look for influence beyond your team: standards other teams adopted, cross-team projects, technical direction for your team. For staff roles, they look for direction across several teams, alignment of senior stakeholders and leaders you developed. If your target level is senior or above, make sure your leadership stories cross team boundaries and make the reach explicit with numbers: teams, people, releases, incidents.

Leadership questions in AI-specific loops

AI teams often add leadership questions shaped by their own pain points: getting research results into production, establishing evaluation and safety practices, and coordinating between model providers, platform teams and product teams. Expect questions such as “How did you get a research prototype into production?” or “How did you establish an evaluation process the team actually follows?”. Both are influence questions in disguise: researchers and product teams rarely report to the engineer making the change. Having one story ready for each is worth the preparation time.

The follow-ups to prepare

Leadership stories attract follow-ups about the people side: Who resisted, and why? What did they say? What would you have done if they had said no? How did you decide who to involve first? Who else deserves credit? What happened after you moved on; did it last? How did the people you led feel about it? Prepare honest, specific answers for each leadership story. The last two are especially telling: a change that lasted after you left and a team that would work with you again are the best evidence of real leadership.
myths: Leadership questions are only for people who have managed a team.

Google’s structured-interview guide describes looking for “emergent leadership” in individual contributors (taking initiative and working collaboratively across teams), and its candidate tips mention helping a team succeed even when you were not officially the leader. Leading a project, setting a standard others adopt and mentoring are all leadership evidence.
Influence means being persuasive in meetings.

Most durable influence happens outside meetings: understanding what the other team needs, writing a clear case with evidence, running a pilot, and doing the work that makes adoption cheap. Persuasive talk without those things rarely changes what people do.
A good influence story is one where everyone agreed immediately.

If nobody resisted, there was no influence to show. Strong stories contain real resistance or indifference, describe the other side’s reasons fairly, and show what you did that changed their minds or their incentives.
Leading means making the decisions.

Leading a project often means making sure decisions get made by the right people, at the right time, with the right information, and that everyone knows what was decided. A lead who makes every decision personally becomes a bottleneck.
Taking credit for the team’s success shows leadership.

Leaders are judged by what happens through other people. Describing what you did to enable others, and crediting them by name or role, is stronger evidence than claiming the outcome. Interviewers also check whether you were genuinely the driver, so be precise about your part.
Mentoring stories are soft and do not count as impact.

Developing people is one of the core expectations Google’s manager research identifies, and for senior individual contributors it is part of the job. A mentoring story with a concrete starting point, specific actions and a visible change in the other person’s work is strong leadership evidence.
lab:
Goal: prepare one influence story and check it uses the real levers of influence. Time: about 40 minutes.

  1. Find candidates. List three times you got people who did not report to you to do something differently: adopt a tool, change a process, reprioritise, accept a design. Pick the one with the most genuine resistance.
  2. Draw the stakeholder map. Place each person involved by influence and by how much the change affected them. Mark who decided, who could block and who were allies.
  3. Write their position. For the main resistant party, write in two sentences what they were measured on and why the change was unattractive to them at first.
  4. Check the levers. For each of the six levers (credibility, their incentives, evidence in their terms, a written case, lowering the cost of yes, allies and credit), write what you did, or “nothing”. A strong story has at least three.
  5. Find the number. Write the adoption result and its effect: teams, releases, incidents, time.
  6. Draft and record a STAR answer of about two and a half minutes. Check that no sentence says “I convinced” or “I told” without saying how.

Finally, ask yourself whether the person you influenced would recognise your account of it. If not, revise until they would.

What to look for: if your levers column shows only “evidence” and “a presentation”, your story is persuasion, not influence. Look for what you did to lower the other side’s cost or to make the win theirs; if you did nothing like that, consider a different story.
recap: For individual contributors, leadership means getting things done through people you have no authority over: other teams, researchers, product managers and peers.
Start by mapping the people involved: who decides, who is affected, who can block, and what each of them is measured on and worried about.
Build the case in writing with evidence framed in their terms, address their objections directly, and propose a small pilot rather than a big commitment.
Lower the cost of saying yes by doing the hard first part yourself, starting with one willing team and letting their success persuade the next.
Credibility comes from expertise, a record of delivering, being dependable and giving credit; it is built before you need it.
Leading a project without being a manager means making goals, roles, decisions and progress clear and removing blockers, not doing all the work or making every call.
Developing others counts: a good mentoring story shows a specific starting point, what you did and a visible change in the other person’s work.
A strong influence story has real resistance, a fair account of the other side, your specific moves, a measured adoption result and shared credit.

drill:
Plan the influence

You are an AI engineer on a product team. You believe the company should route all LLM calls through a shared gateway that logs prompts and responses (with personal data redacted), enforces cost limits and allows model switching. Four product teams call model providers directly from their own code, each in a different way. You have no authority over them, and your manager supports the idea but will not mandate it. Plan how you would get the teams to adopt the gateway, and say how you would tell it later as an interview story.

Answer

Map the people: the four teams’ tech leads (affected, must change code), their PMs (care about launch speed), security and privacy (would strongly want logging and redaction: likely allies or even sponsors), finance or whoever watches LLM spend (ally), and a platform team that might eventually own the gateway (needed for long-term support). Learn each team’s incentives and blockers: likely fear of added latency, fear of a dependency on an unproven service, and migration effort.

Build credibility and evidence: measure the current state (spend per team, incidents caused by provider outages or unexpected model changes, absence of logs in any recent incident investigation). Write a short design document with options (do nothing, shared library, gateway), the trade-offs (added latency, a new single point of failure and how you would mitigate it), and a small ask. Get security or privacy to review it; their support carries weight.

Lower the cost of yes: build the gateway to be a drop-in replacement for the provider client library, keep the added latency to a few milliseconds and measure it, offer to make the migration change for the first team yourself, and run in pass-through mode first. Start with the team that suffered most from a recent incident. Let their tech lead share the result. Then agree with the platform team who will own it long-term, so other teams are not depending on one person.

As an interview story: open with the problem and the lack of authority; spend the action time on understanding each team’s concerns, the written case with security’s support, the drop-in design and first migration, and the champion-led spread; give a result (teams migrated, spend visibility, an incident resolved faster because logs existed, cost saved by limits); credit the first team’s lead and the platform team; and end with a lesson such as “find the ally whose goals your proposal serves most, and do the first migration yourself.”
qa: E
Tell me about a time you led a project.

Describe the project and your role, what made it need leadership (several people, unclear plan, dependencies), and what you did as the lead: set the goal and plan, clarified roles, made sure decisions got made and recorded, kept people informed, removed blockers, and handled a problem along the way. Give the measured outcome and credit others. A strong answer shows enabling others, not doing everything personally.
Follow-up: What was the hardest part of leading it? — Name a real difficulty, such as a dependency slipping or a disagreement on the team, and what you did.
E
Tell me about a time you influenced someone without having authority over them.

Pick a case with real resistance: another team, a researcher or a PM who had reasons not to change. Explain their position fairly, then your moves: understanding their incentives, building a written case with evidence in their terms, offering a pilot, doing work that lowered their cost. End with the measured adoption result and what you learned about influence.
E
What does leadership mean for an individual contributor?

Getting good outcomes through other people without formal authority: taking initiative on problems nobody owns, setting technical direction others follow, raising the standard of the team’s work, helping colleagues grow, and working across teams to get things done. Google describes this as emergent leadership. A strong answer then gives a short real example.
M
Tell me about a time you got another team to adopt a tool or standard you built.

Show the adoption problem honestly (why they did not want to), how you learned what they needed, what you changed or offered to lower their cost, the pilot and its evidence, and how adoption spread. Include a number: teams adopted, share of releases gated, time saved. Credit the champion on the other team.
Follow-up: Did any team refuse? — If one did, say why and what you did; accepting a good reason not to adopt is a mature result.
M
How do you convince a product manager to prioritise technical work, such as evaluation infrastructure, over a new feature?

Translate the technical work into the PM’s outcomes: the risk it removes (regressions, incidents, delays) and the speed it adds to future features, with numbers from past incidents or releases. Propose a small first step with a visible result. Accept that it is their prioritisation call and agree on a decision, rather than arguing indefinitely. A strong answer includes a real example where this worked or did not.
Follow-up: And if they still say no? — Ask what evidence would change their mind, look for a smaller version that fits, and revisit when that evidence appears.
M
How do you build credibility with a new team quickly?

Listen first and learn their goals and pain points; deliver something small and useful early; be reliable on commitments; be precise about what you know and do not know; and give credit generously. Credibility is mostly built before you need to influence anyone, so a strong answer describes deliberate early steps rather than relying on title or expertise alone.
M
Tell me about a time you mentored someone.

Describe the person’s starting point specifically (for example, a new engineer who struggled to scope work), what you did (regular sessions, pairing, giving them a stretch task with support, specific feedback), how you adjusted to them, and the visible change in their work, ideally confirmed by them or their manager. A strong answer shows you developed their judgement rather than solving their problems for them.
Follow-up: What did you learn from mentoring them? — Something specific about your own explanations or habits, which shows the reflection is real.
M
How do you lead a project when some contributors are more senior than you?

Be clear that your role is to make the project work, not to outrank anyone: agree goals and roles at the start, ask for their expertise explicitly, make decisions transparent with a decision log, and route decisions in their area to them. Earn trust by being well prepared and dependable. A strong answer shows comfort leading through clarity rather than authority.
H
Tell me about a time you tried to influence a decision and failed.

Describe the decision, your case, the other side’s reasons, what you tried and why it did not work. Then show a mature response: you committed to the decision, and you reflected on what was missing, such as evidence framed in their terms, involving them earlier, or a smaller ask. If the decision later proved right or wrong, say what you did with that. Interviewers value this because it shows influence is a skill you analyse.
Follow-up: What would you do differently? — Name a specific change, such as starting with a pilot or talking to the decision owner earlier.
H
How do you influence a research team to change how they evaluate models before release?

Start from their goals: they want their models to succeed and their results to hold up. Show concrete cases where the current evaluation missed real production failures, framed as risks to their work rather than criticism. Propose an addition rather than a replacement, such as a small production-sampled evaluation set run alongside their benchmarks, and do the work to build and run it. Pilot it on one model, share the results jointly, and let the evidence and their own champions carry it further.
Follow-up: What if they see it as engineering overstepping? — Make them co-owners: invite them to design the evaluation with you, and credit it to the joint effort.
H
What is the difference between influence and manipulation?

Influence changes someone’s decision by giving them better information, aligning the proposal with their real interests, and making it easier to act, all in the open; they would agree with how they were persuaded if they saw it. Manipulation relies on hiding information, exploiting pressure or bias, or misrepresenting the evidence. A strong answer adds that influence based on manipulation fails in the long run because it destroys the credibility future influence depends on.
H
How does leadership differ at senior and staff levels for an AI engineer?

At senior level, leadership usually means leading projects and setting technical direction within a team, raising its standards (for example how it evaluates models), and mentoring. At staff level, it extends across teams: choosing which problems the organisation should solve, setting shared standards and architecture, aligning research, product and engineering, and developing other leaders. Stories should show scope accordingly: decisions that changed what several teams did, and practices that outlived your involvement.

t: “Why this company, why this role” and questions to ask the interviewer
sum: A strong “why us” answer joins three things: specific, verified facts about the work, your own trajectory, and what you would bring. And the questions you ask at the end are both evidence about you and your best chance to judge the team. How to research, answer and ask.
prereq: beh3
Your intro has a present–past–future shape; the future part already says in two sentences why this role is your next step.
beh6
Impact is a measured change traced from action to outcome; ownership means caring about results after launch.
why:
Two candidates have performed equally well in a loop for an AI engineer role at a health-technology company. Near the end of the hiring manager’s interview, each is asked, “So why do you want to work here?” The first says: “I’ve always admired the company, you’re a leader in AI, and I love your mission of improving healthcare. I think it would be a great place to grow.” The second says: “I read your engineering blog post about evaluating clinical summaries with physician reviewers, and that’s the problem I’ve been working on from the other side: for the last year I’ve built evaluation for a support assistant, where errors are annoying but not dangerous. I want to work where evaluation has to be that rigorous, and I think the release-gating approach I built would carry over.” The hiring manager will remember the second candidate. (Both candidates, and the company, are illustrative examples.)

“Why this company?” and “why this role?” are among the most predictable questions in any loop, and among the most often wasted. Candidates prepare their technical stories carefully and then improvise motivation, which produces generic praise that could be said to any employer. Interviewers ask the question for real reasons. They want to know whether you will stay and care: people who chose a role for specific reasons tend to be more engaged than people who applied everywhere. They want to see whether you did your homework, because research before a decision is a habit they want on the job. And they want to check whether what you want matches what the role actually offers, since a mismatch means an unhappy hire.

The end of the interview has a second, related moment: “Do you have any questions for me?” This is not politeness. Google’s guidance to candidates puts it directly: “Interviewing is a two-way street, so come prepared with questions… This is your opportunity to interview us as well. Both sides need to be a fit!” Your questions are evidence about how you think, and the answers are your best evidence about whether you want the job. Many candidates ask nothing, or ask something answered on the careers page, and leave knowing no more than when they arrived.

This lesson covers both moments. It explains what interviewers listen for, how to research a company using official sources only (and why that matters), how to build a 45–60 second “why us” from three ingredients, and the related questions about why you are leaving and why AI. It then turns to your questions: what to ask each kind of interviewer, AI-specific questions that reveal how a team really works, what not to ask, and how to use the answers to decide. The worked example is a weak and a strong answer to “Why do you want to work here?”, annotated sentence by sentence.
primer:
Think of a good “why us” answer as the intersection of three circles. The first circle is your trajectory: what you have done and what you want to do next. The second is the role’s actual work: what this team builds, the problems it faces, what the job description says the person will do. The third is specific, verified facts you learned about the company and team: a blog post, a paper, a product feature, something the recruiter told you. A strong answer sits where all three overlap.

Each circle on its own produces a recognisable weak answer. Only your trajectory: “I want to grow and learn new things” (true of every job). Only the role: a recitation of the job description back to the interviewer. Only facts about the company: “You were founded in 2012, you have 3,000 employees and you recently launched an AI product”, which shows research but not motivation. Two circles are better; all three make an answer that could only be said by you, to this company, for this role.

The analogy also tells you what preparation looks like. You already have the first circle from your story bank and intro. The second comes from reading the job description closely and asking the recruiter what the team actually does. The third, verified specifics, is the one most candidates skip, and it is the one that takes real effort: reading what the company has published about its work and using the product.

Why does the third circle matter so much? Because it is the only one an interviewer can check, and the only one that costs effort. Anyone can claim to be motivated and anyone can read the job title; only someone who actually spent time on the company’s published work can say something specific and true about it. Interviewers treat that effort as a proxy for how you will approach decisions on the job: an engineer who researched a team before asking to join it is likely to research a problem before proposing a solution. This is also why a single precise fact beats a list of vague ones. “Your post on physician review of summaries” is worth more than “you do a lot of interesting things in healthcare AI”, because it proves you read something, and invites a real conversation about it.

There is a second, quieter benefit. Doing the research changes your own view. Sometimes it makes you more excited about the role; sometimes it reveals that the work is not what you want. Either outcome is valuable before you spend a day in interviews.

The questions you ask at the end work the same way. A question that sits in the same overlap (“Your blog described physician review for clinical summaries; how does that scale as the number of summary types grows?”) shows research, technical thinking and genuine interest all at once. It also gets you information you need, which is the other half of the point.
body:
1. What interviewers are judging

Motivation questions take several forms: why this company, why this role, why now, why are you leaving, why AI, what are you looking for in your next role. Interviewers use them to judge four things.

  • Motivation fit: whether what drives you matches what the role offers. Someone who wants to do research will be unhappy in a role that is mostly integration work, however enthusiastic they sound.
  • Likelihood of staying and caring: a specific reason to choose this role predicts engagement better than general enthusiasm.
  • Research habits: did you find out about the work before asking to join it? Preparing well for a decision is a habit teams want.
  • Honesty: interviewers have heard every flattering formula; an answer that sounds true is worth more than one that sounds polished.

Amazon’s candidate guide describes “Why Amazon?” as a common question whose answer “helps us get a better sense of who you are and what motivates you”, and suggests thinking about “what excites you about the role and the team (or teams) you’ll be meeting with”. Note the emphasis on the role and the team, not the company in general.

2. Researching the company: official sources only

The third circle needs facts, and the quality of the facts matters. Use sources the company itself has published or that come from the people doing the work:

SourceWhat it gives you
Job descriptionThe responsibilities and requirements, often with hints about current problems (“help us scale our evaluation infrastructure”).
Engineering blog and conference talksHow the team builds things, what they are proud of, what problems they have written about.
Research papers, model cards, technical reportsFor AI companies: what models they build, how they evaluate them, the limitations they acknowledge.
Product documentation and the product itselfWhat the product actually does, and where it is strong or weak. Use it before the interview.
Responsible-AI, safety or privacy pagesThe practices and commitments the company states publicly.
Annual reports, shareholder letters, official announcementsCompany direction and priorities, for public companies.
The recruiterWhat the team works on, how the loop is structured, what the hiring manager cares about. Ask directly.
Current or former employeesDay-to-day reality, if you can reach them; treat as one person’s view.

Two rules keep this honest. First, only state as fact what you have verified, and say where you learned it: “I read in your engineering blog that…” is safe; “I heard you’re rebuilding your whole platform” is a rumour, and repeating it can embarrass you or the interviewer. Second, do not over-claim: reading one blog post does not make you an expert on the team, and interviewers can tell when a candidate is stretching a single fact. It is fine to say what you do not know and ask about it; that is often the best transition into a good question.

3. Building the answer: three parts in under a minute

A strong “why us” answer usually has three parts and takes 45–60 seconds.

  1. The specific thing (about 15 seconds): what about this team’s work draws you, named concretely. “Your team owns evaluation and release for every model the company ships” or “the post your team wrote about grounding answers in contracts”.
  2. Why it matters to you (about 20 seconds): the connection to your trajectory, ideally to a story in your bank. “I built evaluation for one product and found it was the part that decided whether we could ship; I want to work on it at a larger scale.”
  3. What you would bring (about 15 seconds): the contribution, not a list of skills. “The approach I used, gating releases on production-sampled evaluation sets, would apply directly to the multi-product setting.”

Then stop. The answer is short because it does not need to prove everything; it needs to sound specific and true, and to invite a follow-up conversation about the team’s work, which is usually where the interviewer goes next.

Notice what is not in the structure: prestige (“it’s a top company”), perks, compensation, and flattery (“you’re the leader in AI”). Those may be real considerations for you, and that is fine, but as the main answer they say nothing about fit. Mission statements are a special case: quoting the company’s mission back to it is flattery unless you connect it to something concrete you have done or seen.

4. The related motivation questions

Why this role (versus another role at the company)? Focus on the work itself: what the role does day to day, and why that suits your trajectory. If you are applying for an AI engineer role rather than a research scientist role, for example, be able to say why building and shipping is what you want.

Why are you leaving your current job? beh3 covers this: one or two honest, forward-looking sentences about what you are moving toward, never criticism of your employer. It should connect naturally to your “why us”.

Why AI engineering? The bank question on this theme gives the shape: “a concrete arc: a problem you hit, what you built, what it taught you, and what you want to do next. Specific beats enthusiastic.” Interest in AI is near-universal among candidates, so the only thing that distinguishes you is the specific path that led you here.

What are you looking for in your next role? Answer honestly with two or three specific things (the kind of problem, the kind of team, the kind of growth), and make sure they are things this role offers. If they are not, that is worth knowing before you accept.

5. Questions to ask: what they are for

Your questions do two jobs at once. They are evidence: a thoughtful, specific question shows research, technical judgement and real interest; Google’s guidance says having questions prepared “shows you care about understanding Google and the position… and is a testament to the research you’ve done”. And they are information: the answers are the best data you will get about whether you want to work there. Of the two, the second matters more in the long run. A job that looked good from outside and turns out to be constant firefighting under an unclear manager is a costly mistake, and the interview loop is your chance to find out.

Amazon’s guide notes that interviewers try to leave a few minutes at the end for questions, and that if time runs out you can follow up with your recruiting contact. In practice you usually have five minutes or less. Prepare three to five questions for each interviewer so you can choose the best one or two for the time available, and do not use the time on things you could have read online.

6. What to ask each kind of interviewer

Different people can answer different questions well. Tailor your questions to the interviewer’s role.

InterviewerGood questions
RecruiterHow is the loop structured and what does each round assess? What level is this role, and how is level decided? Is there team matching after the loop? What is the timeline?
Hiring managerWhat does success look like at six months and a year? What is the biggest challenge the team faces right now? How are priorities set and decisions made? How do people on the team grow?
Peer engineerWhat does a typical week look like? How do code review, deployment and on-call work? What do you wish you had known when you joined? What would you change?
Researcher or PMHow do research results get into production? How do engineering, research and product disagree, and how are disagreements settled? How is success of an AI feature measured?
Skip-level or leaderWhere is the team’s work heading in the next year or two? How does this team’s work connect to the company’s priorities? What would make you consider this hire a great success?

7. AI-specific questions that reveal how a team works

For AI engineering roles, a handful of questions are unusually revealing because the answers expose whether the team has mature practices or is improvising.

  • “How do you decide a model or prompt change is ready to ship?” A good answer mentions an evaluation set, ideally drawn from real usage, and some form of staged rollout. “We try it and see” tells you a lot.
  • “What happens when a model provider updates a model you depend on?” Reveals whether they pin versions, re-evaluate, and monitor.
  • “How do you know an AI feature is working for users after launch?” Reveals monitoring and the metrics they trust.
  • “How does work move from research or prototype to production here?” Reveals how the groups collaborate, and where friction is.
  • “What was the last significant incident with an AI feature, and what changed afterwards?” Reveals whether they learn from failure (beh5).
  • “What is hardest about this work right now?” An honest, specific answer is a good sign; a vague one is a mild warning.

These questions also showcase your own knowledge without boasting: asking how a team handles provider model updates tells the interviewer you know that is a real problem.

8. What not to ask, and how to ask well

Avoid questions answered on the company’s website or in the job description (they show no research), “How did I do?” or “Did I pass?” (interviewers usually cannot say, and it puts them in an awkward spot), detailed compensation questions with interviewers (the recruiter handles those; beh10 covers when), and questions framed as accusations (“Why is your app so slow?”). Avoid long lists: two good questions with real follow-up beat five in rapid succession.

How you ask matters as much as what. Ask open questions (“how”, “what”, “tell me about”), not yes/no. Listen and follow up: “You mentioned evaluation is mostly manual right now; is automating it part of this role?” turns a scripted question into a conversation and shows you were listening. Take brief notes, because you will want to compare answers later. And watch the clock: if the interviewer has given you five minutes, do not take fifteen.

9. Using the answers to decide

Keep notes on what each interviewer said and compare them after the loop. Useful signals include: whether success in the role is defined clearly and consistently; whether the team has evaluation, monitoring and on-call practices or lives in constant firefighting; whether decisions are made transparently and by clear owners; whether people describe the same priorities; and whether people seem to enjoy working together. Google’s team effectiveness research is a handy checklist here: psychological safety, dependability, structure and clarity, meaning and impact are all things you can ask about.

Some answers are red flags: nobody can say what success looks like; three interviewers give three different top priorities; every story involves an emergency; questions about evaluation get a shrug; the hiring manager speaks badly of other teams. None is decisive alone, but together they predict your experience. If you get an offer, you can usually ask follow-up questions of the hiring manager or recruiter before deciding, and you should.

10. “What other companies are you talking to?”

Recruiters, and occasionally interviewers, ask whether you are interviewing elsewhere. The question is legitimate: they want to understand your timeline and how competitive the process is. You are not obliged to name companies, and naming them rarely helps you at this stage. A good answer is honest and general: “Yes, I’m in process with a few companies, mostly for AI engineering roles focused on evaluation and production LLM systems, and I expect to be making decisions in the next three or four weeks.” That tells the recruiter what they need (you are actively looking, what you are looking for, and your timeline) and connects your search to your stated motivation.

Two things to avoid. Do not pretend you are not looking elsewhere if you are; if an offer timeline later forces you to say so, the earlier answer looks dishonest. And do not inflate your other processes to create pressure; recruiters talk to many candidates and can usually tell. If you have a real deadline from another company, telling the recruiter early is in your interest, because many companies can speed up their process when they know (beh10 covers this in the offer stage).

11. Worked example: “Why do you want to work here?”

The candidate and company below are illustrative examples written for this lesson. The company, “Northwind Health”, is fictional; imagine it publishes an engineering blog describing how physicians review AI-generated clinical note summaries before release. The role is an AI engineer on its clinical summarisation team.

Weak answer (about 45 seconds):

What the candidate saysWhat the interviewer writesSignal or noise
“I’ve always been really impressed by Northwind, you’re clearly one of the leaders in healthcare AI.”“Flattery.”Noise: could be said to any company in the field.
“And I love your mission of making healthcare better for everyone.”“Quotes mission.”Noise: no connection to the candidate.
“I’m really passionate about AI and I want to work somewhere I can grow and learn from smart people.”“Generic motivation.”Noise: true of every job.
“Plus I heard you’re planning a big expansion next year, so it seems like a great time to join.”“Rumour re: expansion.”Negative: unverified, and may make the interviewer uncomfortable.

Strong answer (about 55 seconds):

What the candidate saysWhat the interviewer writesSignal or noise
(Specific thing, 15 s) “I read your team’s blog post on how physicians review summaries before a model ships, and it described exactly the problem I care about: deciding when an LLM is good enough to release.”“Read our eval blog post; cares about release decisions.”Signal: verified, specific, with its source.
(Why it matters to me, 20 s) “For the last year I’ve owned evaluation for a support assistant, and I built a release gate on real conversations. But in support, a wrong answer is annoying; in clinical summaries, it can harm someone. I want to work where evaluation has to be that rigorous.”“Owns eval + release gate. Wants higher-stakes eval.”Strong signal: trajectory connects to the team’s work; motivation is about the work.
(What I’d bring, 15 s) “I think the way I sampled real traffic and tracked factual errors would carry over, and I’d want to learn how you scale expert review, because physician time is expensive.”“Would bring: production-sampled eval, factual-error tracking. Curious about scaling expert review.”Signal: specific contribution plus a genuine question that opens discussion.
(Close, 5 s) “That’s the main reason. It’s the work.”“Clear, sincere.”Signal: clean ending.

The strong answer is barely longer than the weak one. It names something real and checkable, connects it to the candidate’s own record, says what they would contribute, and raises a natural question (how physician review scales) that the hiring manager will probably want to talk about. That last move matters: a good “why us” answer often turns into the most engaged conversation of the interview.

A good question for the end of the same interview might be: “When a summary type passes physician review, how do you monitor it after release, given that the notes it sees keep changing?” It sits in the same overlap of research, technical judgement and interest, and the answer tells the candidate whether the team’s rigour continues after launch.
deep:
Motivation fit and why companies care

Companies care about motivation for practical reasons. Hiring is expensive, the first months in a role are mostly cost, and an engineer who leaves after a year because the work was not what they wanted is a loss for both sides. Specific motivation is a reasonable, if imperfect, predictor that the match is good: if you can say exactly what about the work attracts you, and the role really offers it, you are more likely to stay and do your best work. Generic enthusiasm predicts little, because almost everyone expresses it. This is why interviewers push on vague answers (“what specifically about our team?”): they are trying to find out whether there is a real match underneath.

Honesty when the reasons are mixed

Real motivations are usually mixed: the work is interesting, the pay is better, the location suits you, a friend works there, you need to leave your current job. You do not need to list them all, and you should not pretend the interesting work is the only reason if it is not. The honest approach is to lead with the reasons that are both true and relevant to the role, which for any role worth taking should include something about the work, and to leave out reasons that are true but irrelevant to the interviewer. What you must avoid is inventing reasons, especially fabricated specifics (“I’ve followed your work for years”) that a single follow-up question would expose.

When the company is controversial or in the news

AI companies are often in the news, sometimes for difficult reasons: safety debates, legal cases, reorganisations, layoffs. Do not raise news stories you have not verified, and do not offer opinions on controversies unless asked. If an interviewer raises a public topic, or you genuinely need to understand something to decide (for example, how a reorganisation affects the team), ask a calm, open question in the right setting, usually with the hiring manager or recruiter: “I saw the announcement about the reorganisation; how does it affect this team’s plans?” This gets you real information without putting the interviewer on the defensive.

Why your questions are evaluated

Interviewers form impressions from your questions even when they are not formally scored. Specific questions grounded in research signal preparation. Questions about how decisions are made, how quality is measured and what is hard signal the kind of engineer who thinks about the system around the code. Questions only about perks, remote work or promotion speed, asked first, can signal priorities that worry an interviewer, even though they are legitimate concerns; ask them of the recruiter, or later. And the way you listen to answers (following up, connecting to what you heard earlier) is evidence of the collaboration skills the whole loop is trying to measure.

Startups and large companies call for different questions

The same question can matter very differently depending on the company’s size and stage. At a large company, the biggest unknowns are usually about the specific team: who the manager is, what the team owns, how it fits into the larger organisation, and how much of your time will go to process. At a startup, the unknowns are about the company itself: how long its funding lasts, how it makes or plans to make money, whether the product has real users, and how decisions are made when the founders disagree. Questions such as “How do you think about runway and the next funding milestone?” or “What would have to be true in a year for this to be going well?” are normal and appropriate at a startup, usually with a founder or the hiring manager. Asking them calmly signals the maturity that startups need, and the answers can be decisive for your choice.

Judging the manager

Of everything you can learn in an interview loop, the most predictive for your day-to-day experience is probably who your manager will be and how they work. Google’s manager research found that teams with highly effective managers achieved better results, were happier and had lower turnover. You usually meet the hiring manager once, so use the time. Questions that reveal management style include: “How do you give feedback to people on your team?”, “Tell me about someone on your team who grew a lot; what did you do to help?”, “How do you decide what the team works on when there is more to do than people?”, and “What would you want from me in the first month?”. Specific, example-based answers are a good sign; vague answers, or answers that are all about the manager’s own achievements, are worth noting.

Team matching and choosing between teams

At some large companies, candidates pass a general loop and then talk to several teams in a team matching stage before an offer is finalised. These conversations are interviews in both directions: the team is checking fit, and you are choosing where you will spend the next few years. Everything in this lesson applies with more weight. A specific “why this team” answer helps you get matched where you want, and the questions you ask (about the manager’s style, the team’s practices, the work you would own) are your main source of information for the choice. Ask the recruiter in advance how matching works and how many teams you can talk to.
prod:
How these answers go wrong

The flattery answer. “You’re the best company in AI.” Says nothing about you. Fix: name the specific work and connect it to your trajectory.

The mission quote. Reciting the mission statement. Fix: if the mission genuinely matters to you, connect it to something concrete you have done or seen.

The prestige and perks answer. “It would be great for my career”, “the benefits are amazing”. Fix: keep those private; lead with the work.

The rumour. Repeating forum gossip or guesses about internal plans. Fix: use only official sources, and say where you learned it.

The over-claim. “I know your stack inside out” after reading one post. Fix: say what you read and ask about what you do not know.

No questions. “No, I think you’ve covered everything.” Fix: always have at least two prepared per interviewer.

The website question. “What does your company do?” Fix: research first; ask about what research could not tell you.

The interrogation. Five rapid questions with no follow-up. Fix: fewer questions, listen, follow up.

A preparation routine

For each company, budget about two hours. Read the job description twice and underline the responsibilities and any hints about current problems. Read two or three recent engineering blog posts or talks from the relevant team or area, and for AI companies their model documentation or responsible-AI pages. Use the product for twenty minutes. Write a 45–60 second “why us” in the three-part structure, checking every fact against its source. Write three to five questions for each interviewer you know about, at least one of them following from your research. Finally, check that your “why us” is consistent with your intro’s future part (beh3) and your answer to why you are leaving.

Following up after the interview

If you ran out of time for questions, or thought of one later, Amazon’s guidance explicitly suggests following up through your recruiting contact. A short, specific follow-up to the recruiter (“I didn’t get to ask about how the team handles provider model updates; is there someone I could ask, or could you pass it on?”) is perfectly normal. Thank-you notes vary by company and culture; a brief, sincere note to the recruiter is never wrong, but do not expect it to change a decision. What matters more is collecting the answers you need before you have to decide on an offer, which beh10 covers.

Using the questions to protect yourself

It is easy to treat the end of the interview as a formality while you are anxious about passing. Try to remember that you are also deciding. A role at a famous company on a team with no evaluation practice, unclear ownership and a manager who cannot describe success can be a worse career move than a role at a smaller company with a clear mandate and good practices. The questions in this lesson are designed to surface those differences, and asking them calmly and specifically also happens to make you a more impressive candidate.
myths: “Why do you want to work here?” is a formality.

Interviewers use it to judge motivation (will you stay and care?), how much research you did, and whether your goals fit the role. Amazon’s candidate guide calls “Why Amazon?” a common question that helps them understand what motivates you. A generic answer is a mild negative; a specific, honest one can separate you from an otherwise equal candidate.
The best answer praises the company’s mission and reputation.

Flattery and mission-statement quotes carry no information, because every candidate can say them. A strong answer names specific work the team does, connects it to what you have done and want to do next, and says what you would contribute.
It is fine to say what you have heard about the company even if you have not checked it.

Repeating rumours, forum posts or guesses about internal plans can embarrass you if they are wrong and can look like gossip if they are right. Use facts from official sources (the company’s blog, papers, documentation, talks, the product itself) and say where you learned them.
Asking no questions at the end is safe.

Google’s candidate guidance says having questions prepared shows you care about understanding the company and the position. No questions can read as lack of interest or preparation, and you lose your best chance to judge whether you want the job.
Good questions are clever questions designed to impress.

The best questions are ones you genuinely need answered to decide, asked well: specific, open, and followed up. Questions designed only to impress tend to sound rehearsed, and interviewers notice when you do not listen to the answer.
You should ask every interviewer the same questions.

Different interviewers can answer different things. Ask a recruiter about process and level, a hiring manager about expectations and team challenges, a peer engineer about daily practice, and leadership about direction. Asking the same question of two people can be useful deliberately, to compare answers.
lab:
Goal: prepare a “why us” answer and a question set for one real target company. Time: about 90 minutes, mostly research.

  1. Research (45 min). Read the job description and underline responsibilities and problems. Read two or three recent official posts, talks or documents from the relevant team. Use the product. For each fact you might use, write the source next to it.
  2. Three circles (10 min). Write three bullets in each circle: your trajectory, the role’s work, verified specifics. Draw lines where items connect across circles.
  3. Write the answer (15 min). Three parts: the specific thing (15 s), why it matters to you (20 s), what you would bring (15 s). Remove every adjective about the company.
  4. Questions (15 min). Write three questions each for the recruiter, hiring manager and a peer engineer, including at least two of the AI-specific questions in this lesson and at least one that follows from your research.
  5. Record and time the answer. Aim for 45–60 seconds. Ask yourself: could another candidate say this word for word to this company? If yes, make it more specific.
  6. Consistency check. Read your intro’s future part and your “why are you leaving” answer next to this one. They should tell one story.

Save the research notes with sources; you will reuse them for the offer decision.

What to look for: the most common gap is the verified-specifics circle. If your answer contains no fact with a source, go back to step 1.
